tasks.title: Classify counting and whole numbers
tasks.objective: Distinguish between counting (natural) numbers and whole numbers.

example.prompt: Counting (natural) numbers start at 1; whole numbers start at 0. For 0, answer: is it a counting number; is it a whole number? Enter yes or no for each, separated by a semicolon.
example.solution: Counting numbers are 1, 2, 3, …; whole numbers include 0 as well. 0 belongs to the whole numbers only.

tasks.title: Name an arithmetic operation
tasks.objective: Identify four fundamental operations of arithmetic.

example.prompt: Name the operation in 18 + 2 = 20. Enter addition, subtraction, multiplication or division.
example.solution: The symbol + means addition.

tasks.title: Name the parts of arithmetic
tasks.objective: Identify and name the parts of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division problems.

example.prompt: In 18 + 6 = 24, name the first number (18). Use the arithmetic term for that part.
example.solution: 18 is an operand called a addend; 6 is an operand called a addend; 24 is the sum.

tasks.title: Write dollars and cents
tasks.objective: Express dollars and cents correctly.

example.prompt: Write 3 cents in dollar notation. Include $ and exactly two decimal places.
example.solution: 100 cents make 1 dollar. 3¢ = $0.03.

tasks.title: Evaluate a variable expression
tasks.objective: Evaluate an expression with variables when the variables are assigned specific values.

example.prompt: Evaluate the expression for x = 3, y = 7, z = 5. Enter an exact fraction, mixed number or terminating decimal.
example.solution: Substitute the given values in ((x × y) + z), follow grouping and multiplication/division before addition/subtraction, and obtain 26.

tasks.title: Multiply whole and decimal numbers
tasks.objective: Multiply with whole and decimal numbers.

example.prompt: Multiply 792 × 42. Enter the exact result as a whole number or decimal.

tasks.title: Divide a decimal by a whole number
tasks.objective: Divide with whole number divisors and decimal number dividends.

example.prompt: Divide 124.525 by 25. Enter the exact decimal quotient.

tasks.title: Give remainder or mixed-number division answers
tasks.objective: Divide with whole number divisors and dividends where the quotient requires a remainder or fraction.

example.prompt: Divide 67 by 11. Use quotient R remainder, for example 3 R 2.

tasks.title: Identify an operation property
tasks.objective: Identify the properties of operations.

example.prompt: Which property is illustrated by 9+2=2+9? Choose: commutative; associative; distributive; additive identity; multiplicative identity; zero multiplication.
example.solution: 9+2=2+9. The order changes, and the result stays the same.

tasks.title: Write an example of an operation property
tasks.objective: Illustrate the properties of operations.

example.prompt: Write a complete numerical equality illustrating the commutative property of addition. Start one side with 3 + 7. Use * or × for multiplication and include =. Reversing the two sides is also accepted.
example.solution: 3+7=7+3. The order changes, and the result stays the same.

tasks.title: State a sequence rule and continue it
tasks.objective: Determine a pattern or rule for a sequence and then apply the rule to continue the sequence.

example.prompt: The sequence changes by a constant amount: 58, 55, 52, 49. State the signed number added each time, then the next three terms. Enter step; next; next; next.
example.solution: Each difference is -3. Add -3 repeatedly to obtain 46, 43, 40.

tasks.title: Write a commutative example
tasks.objective: Illustrate the commutative property of addition or multiplication by giving an example involving specified digits.

example.prompt: Write a complete numerical equality illustrating the commutative property of addition. Start one side with 9 + 3. Use * or × for multiplication and include =. Reversing the two sides is also accepted.
example.solution: 9+3=3+9. The order changes, and the result stays the same.

tasks.title: Write an associative example
tasks.objective: Illustrate the associative property of addition or multiplication by giving an example involving specified digits.

example.prompt: Write a complete numerical equality illustrating the associative property of addition. Use 2, 4, 6 in that order on both sides, changing only the grouping. Use * or × for multiplication and include =. Reversing the two sides is also accepted.
example.solution: (2+4)+6=2+(4+6). Only the grouping changes; the order and result stay the same.

tasks.title: Show a subtraction or division counterexample
tasks.objective: Illustrate why the associative and commutative properties do not apply to the operations of subtraction or division.

example.prompt: Show a counterexample to the commutative property for subtraction. Evaluate 43 − 3; 3 − 43. Enter both exact results, separated by a semicolon.
example.solution: The two results are 40 and -40. They are unequal, so reversing the order does not preserve this result.

tasks.title: Solve a one-operation equation
tasks.objective: Find the value of a variable in addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division equations.

example.prompt: Solve n + 19 = 102. Enter n.
example.solution: Subtract the known addend from 102: n = 83.

tasks.title: Find a missing addend
tasks.objective: Find a missing addend in an equation or number sentence.

example.prompt: Solve n + 12 = 60. Enter n.
example.solution: Subtract the known addend from 60: n = 48.

tasks.title: Find a missing factor
tasks.objective: Find a missing factor in an equation or number sentence.

example.prompt: Solve n × 18 = 1476. Enter n.
example.solution: Divide 1476 by 18: n = 82.

tasks.title: Find a missing minuend or subtrahend
tasks.objective: Find a missing minuend or subtrahend in an equation or number sentence.

example.prompt: Solve n − 18 = 54. Enter n.
example.solution: Add 18 to 54: n = 72.

tasks.title: Find a missing dividend or divisor
tasks.objective: Find a missing divisor or dividend in an equation or number sentence.

example.prompt: Solve n ÷ 6 = 20. Enter n.
example.solution: Multiply 20 by 6: n = 120.

tasks.title: Compare and order points on a number line
tasks.objective: Compare and order numbers on a number line.

example.prompt: Read points A, B and C on the number line. Enter their three numerical values in increasing order, then the symbol comparing A with B. Format: least; middle; greatest; < or >.
example.solution: The values from left to right are -8, 1, 6. A is 1 and B is 6, so A < B.

tasks.title: Compare signed whole numbers
tasks.objective: Use comparison symbols to compare numbers.

example.prompt: Compare -61 and -61. Enter <, > or = to complete -61 ___ -61.
example.solution: Both numbers have the same value.

tasks.title: Add and subtract on a number line
tasks.objective: Add and subtract integers on a number line.

example.prompt: Use the number line to calculate 1 + (-4). The dot is the start; the arrow shows the move. Enter the final value.
example.solution: Start at 1. Adding -4 moves 4 units left, ending at -3.

tasks.title: Name a place through hundred trillions
tasks.objective: Identify the place value of digits in whole numbers to hundred trillions.

example.prompt: In 9, what is the place name of digit 1 from the left (the digit 9)? Count digits only, ignoring commas. For example, use “ten thousands”.
example.solution: There are 0 digit places to its right. Its place is ones (1).

tasks.title: Write expanded notation
tasks.objective: Write whole numbers in expanded notation.

example.prompt: Write 8 in expanded notation as a sum of nonzero place values, greatest first (write 0 for zero). Use +, for example 205 = 200 + 5 (enter only 200 + 5).

tasks.title: Write whole numbers in words
tasks.objective: Read and write whole numbers through hundred trillions in word form.

example.prompt: Write 7 in words. Hyphens and the optional word “and” are accepted.
example.solution: Group the digits in threes from the right: seven.

tasks.title: Write whole numbers from words
tasks.objective: Use digits to express numbers through hundred trillions.

example.prompt: Write this number using digits: five. Commas may be used in groups of three digits.
example.solution: Write each three-digit group in its named position, filling empty places with zeros: 5.

tasks.title: Find a digit value
tasks.objective: Identify the value of a digit in a given place value by multiplying the digit by its place value.

example.prompt: In 3, find the value of digit 1 from the left (the digit 3). Count digits only, ignoring commas. Multiply the digit by its place value and enter the result.

tasks.title: List every factor
tasks.objective: Identify all the factors of a number.

example.prompt: List every positive factor of 1, from least to greatest. Separate answers with semicolons; include 1 and 1, listing a repeated value only once.
example.solution: Factor pairs produce the complete list: 1.

tasks.title: Find the greatest common factor
tasks.objective: Identify the greatest common factor (GCF) of two numbers.

example.prompt: Find the greatest common factor of 108 and 108.
example.solution: The positive common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 27, 36, 54, 108. The greatest is 108.

tasks.title: Apply a divisibility rule
tasks.objective: Test for the divisibility of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10 without performing the division.

example.prompt: Is 842068 divisible by 2? Apply the divisibility rule without dividing 842068: read its last digit. Enter yes/no; rule test value.
example.solution: The test value is 8. This test value must be divisible by 2. Therefore 842068 is divisible by 2.

tasks.title: Identify figures with no dimensions and with one, two, and three dimensions.
tasks.objective: Identify figures with no dimensions and with one, two, and three dimensions.

example.prompt: How many dimensions does a point have? Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: point has no length, width or height.

tasks.title: Define and use symbols to identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles.
tasks.objective: Define and use symbols to identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles.

example.prompt: Draw and label point A. Write its name using standard geometric notation and define the figure. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: A is a location with no size.
example.solution: A is a location with no size. Review: Correct endpoint/arrow/vertex convention. Notation agrees with the labelled drawing. Definition distinguishes the figure from the other types.

tasks.title: Identify two lines in a plane as parallel or intersecting, and if intersecting, then identify the lines as oblique or perpendicular.
tasks.objective: Identify two lines in a plane as parallel or intersecting, and if intersecting, then identify the lines as oblique or perpendicular.

example.prompt: Classify the two lines: parallel, perpendicular, or oblique (intersecting but not perpendicular).
example.solution: The lines remain the same distance apart and do not meet.

tasks.title: Classify angles by their size: acute, obtuse, right, or straight.
tasks.objective: Classify angles by their size: acute, obtuse, right, or straight.

example.prompt: Classify an angle of 110°: acute, right, obtuse or straight.
example.solution: Compare 110° with 90° and 180°: it is obtuse.

tasks.title: Use fractions and percents to name a part of a whole.
tasks.objective: Use fractions and percents to name a part of a whole.

example.prompt: Name the shaded part as a fraction and a percent. Enter fraction; numerical percent. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: 2 of 10 equal parts are shaded: 1/5 = 20%.

tasks.title: Identify the parts of a fraction.
tasks.objective: Identify the parts of a fraction.

example.prompt: In the fraction 4/11, name the role of 11. Enter numerator or denominator.
example.solution: The numerator 4 counts selected parts; denominator 11 specifies equal parts in a whole.

tasks.title: Identify and represent a mixed number on a number line.
tasks.objective: Identify and represent a mixed number on a number line.

example.prompt: Identify the mixed number marked A on the number line. Then draw a second number line and mark 2 1/2 on it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 2 1/2; A is 2.5 units from zero. Review: Correct whole-number interval and fractional subdivision. The drawn point is at the same value.

tasks.title: Read and use percents greater than 100%.
tasks.objective: Read and use percents greater than 100%.

example.prompt: A full tray holds 32 tiles. A collection contains 175% of a full tray. How many tiles is that? Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Use a ruler to measure and draw segments to the nearest sixteenth of an inch.
tasks.objective: Use a ruler to measure and draw segments to the nearest sixteenth of an inch.

example.prompt: Read the marked length on the inch ruler to the nearest 1/16 inch. On paper, use a physical ruler to draw a segment of that length and label it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 2 1/16 inches. Review: Reads the marked tick from the zero baseline. Labels the reduced fractional length. Physical segment agrees within 1/32 inch; do not measure the resized screen drawing.

tasks.title: Identify the precision of a measurement.
tasks.objective: Identify the precision of a measurement.

example.prompt: An inch ruler divides each inch into 2 equal intervals. A reading is rounded to the nearest tick. What is its precision (smallest graduation), in inches? Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).
example.solution: One inch divided by 2 gives 1/2 inch per interval.

tasks.title: Identify a fraction represented by a base ten diagram or other figure.
tasks.objective: Identify a fraction represented by a base ten diagram or other figure.

example.prompt: What fraction of the whole grid is shaded? Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).
example.solution: 72 of 100 cells are shaded: 72/100 = 0.72.

tasks.title: Add fractions with the same denominator; add mixed numbers with the same denominator.
tasks.objective: Add fractions with the same denominator; add mixed numbers with the same denominator.

example.prompt: Add: 3/10 + 9/10. Enter a simplified mixed number, proper fraction or integer.
example.solution: The denominator stays 10. 3 + 9 gives the new numerator; reduce to 1 1/5.

tasks.title: Subtract fractions with the same denominator; subtract mixed numbers with the same denominator.
tasks.objective: Subtract fractions with the same denominator; subtract mixed numbers with the same denominator.

example.prompt: Subtract: 1/3 − 1/3. Enter a simplified mixed number, proper fraction or integer.
example.solution: The denominator stays 3. 1 − 1 gives the new numerator; reduce to 0.

tasks.title: Multiply fractions.
tasks.objective: Multiply fractions.

example.prompt: Multiply 4/5 × 7/12. Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).
example.solution: Multiply numerators and denominators, then reduce: 4×7 / (5×12) = 7/15.

tasks.title: Find the reciprocals of numbers.
tasks.objective: Find the reciprocals of numbers.

example.prompt: Find the reciprocal of 10. Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).
example.solution: Rewrite as 10 and exchange numerator and denominator: 1/10. Their product is 1.

tasks.title: Solve equations using the property that the product of a number and its reciprocal is 1.
tasks.objective: Solve equations using the property that the product of a number and its reciprocal is 1.

example.prompt: Solve (2/5)n = 14 by multiplying both sides by the reciprocal. Show the multiplication and check. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: Multiply both sides by 5/2; n = 35. Substitution gives 2/5 × 35 = 14.
example.solution: Multiply both sides by 5/2; n = 35. Substitution gives 2/5 × 35 = 14. Review: Uses the reciprocal on both sides. Correct exact solution and substitution check.

tasks.title: Use order of operations to simplify expressions involving addition, subtraction, and multiplication of fractions with different denominators.
tasks.objective: Use order of operations to simplify expressions involving addition, subtraction, and multiplication of fractions with different denominators.

example.prompt: Simplify 1/2 + 3/4 × 1/2. Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).
example.solution: Multiply 3/4 by 1/2 first, then add 1/2: 7/8.

tasks.title: Write division answers as mixed numbers.
tasks.objective: Write division answers as mixed numbers.

example.prompt: Divide 12 by 3. Write the answer as a mixed number or whole number. Enter a simplified mixed number, proper fraction or integer.
example.solution: 12 = 3 × 4 + 0; the answer is 4.

tasks.title: Identify improper fractions.
tasks.objective: Identify improper fractions.

example.prompt: Is 1/8 an improper fraction? Use the convention numerator ≥ denominator. Enter yes or no.
example.solution: Compare 1 and 8: numerator is smaller.

tasks.title: Convert an improper fraction to either a whole number or a mixed number.
tasks.objective: Convert an improper fraction to either a whole number or a mixed number.

example.prompt: Rewrite 90/10 as a mixed number or whole number. Enter a simplified mixed number, proper fraction or integer.
example.solution: 90 = 10 × 9 + 0; the answer is 9.

tasks.title: Rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction.
tasks.objective: Rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction.

example.prompt: Write 4 1/2 as an improper fraction. Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).

tasks.title: Solve one-step story problems about combining.
tasks.objective: Solve one-step story problems about combining.

example.prompt: A club has 18 blue counters and 4 red counters. How many counters are there altogether? Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Write equations for story problems about combining.
tasks.objective: Write equations for story problems about combining.

example.prompt: A club has 18 blue counters and 8 red counters. How many counters are there altogether? Write an equation using n for the unknown, then solve it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: 18 + 8 = n; n = 26. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted.
example.solution: 18 + 8 = n; n = 26. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted. Review: Equation models the quantities and unknown in the story. The solution includes the correct quantity.

tasks.title: Write story problems with addition patterns.
tasks.objective: Write story problems with addition patterns.

example.prompt: Write your own one-step story problem modeled by 58 + 3 = n. Define what n represents and solve your problem. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: One valid example: A club has 58 blue counters and 3 red counters. How many counters are there altogether? Answer: 61.
example.solution: One valid example: A club has 58 blue counters and 3 red counters. How many counters are there altogether? Answer: 61. Review: Story quantities match the equation and requested relationship. Unknown is meaningful and explicitly stated. Solution is 61 with an appropriate unit.

tasks.title: Solve one-step story problems about separating.
tasks.objective: Solve one-step story problems about separating.

example.prompt: A club has 37 counters and gives away 3. How many remain? Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Write equations for story problems about separating.
tasks.objective: Write equations for story problems about separating.

example.prompt: A club has 49 counters and gives away 2. How many remain? Write an equation using n for the unknown, then solve it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: 49 - 2 = n; n = 47. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted.
example.solution: 49 - 2 = n; n = 47. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted. Review: Equation models the quantities and unknown in the story. The solution includes the correct quantity.

tasks.title: Write story problems with subtraction patterns.
tasks.objective: Write story problems with subtraction patterns.

example.prompt: Write your own one-step story problem modeled by 47 - 4 = n. Define what n represents and solve your problem. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: One valid example: A club has 47 counters and gives away 4. How many remain? Answer: 43.
example.solution: One valid example: A club has 47 counters and gives away 4. How many remain? Answer: 43. Review: Story quantities match the equation and requested relationship. Unknown is meaningful and explicitly stated. Solution is 43 with an appropriate unit.

tasks.title: Solve one-step story problems about comparing.
tasks.objective: Solve one-step story problems about comparing.

example.prompt: Ari has 14 cards. Bo has 21 cards. How many more does Bo have than Ari? Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Write equations for story problems about comparing.
tasks.objective: Write equations for story problems about comparing.

example.prompt: Ari has 13 cards. Bo has 21 cards. How many more does Bo have than Ari? Write an equation using n for the unknown, then solve it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: 21 - 13 = n; n = 8. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted.
example.solution: 21 - 13 = n; n = 8. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted. Review: Equation models the quantities and unknown in the story. The solution includes the correct quantity.

tasks.title: Write story problems that are about comparing.
tasks.objective: Write story problems that are about comparing.

example.prompt: Write your own one-step story problem modeled by 42 - 40 = n. Define what n represents and solve your problem. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: One valid example: Ari has 40 cards. Bo has 42 cards. How many more does Bo have than Ari? Answer: 2.
example.solution: One valid example: Ari has 40 cards. Bo has 42 cards. How many more does Bo have than Ari? Answer: 2. Review: Story quantities match the equation and requested relationship. Unknown is meaningful and explicitly stated. Solution is 2 with an appropriate unit.

tasks.title: Solve one-step story problems about elapsed time.
tasks.objective: Solve one-step story problems about elapsed time.

example.prompt: A lesson starts at 8:00 a.m. and ends at 9:25 a.m.. How many minutes pass? Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Count from 8:00 a.m. to 9:25 a.m.: 85 minutes.

tasks.title: Solve one-step story problems about equal groups.
tasks.objective: Solve one-step story problems about equal groups.

example.prompt: There are 3 equal boxes with 48 pencils in each. How many pencils are there? Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Write equations for story problems about equal groups.
tasks.objective: Write equations for story problems about equal groups.

example.prompt: There are 7 equal boxes with 26 pencils in each. How many pencils are there? Write an equation using n for the unknown, then solve it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: 7 × 26 = n; n = 182. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted.
example.solution: 7 × 26 = n; n = 182. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted. Review: Equation models the quantities and unknown in the story. The solution includes the correct quantity.

tasks.title: Write story problems about equal groups.
tasks.objective: Write story problems about equal groups.

example.prompt: Write your own one-step story problem modeled by 6 × 46 = n. Define what n represents and solve your problem. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: One valid example: There are 6 equal boxes with 46 pencils in each. How many pencils are there? Answer: 276.
example.solution: One valid example: There are 6 equal boxes with 46 pencils in each. How many pencils are there? Answer: 276. Review: Story quantities match the equation and requested relationship. Unknown is meaningful and explicitly stated. Solution is 276 with an appropriate unit.

tasks.title: Solve one-step story problems about parts of a whole.
tasks.objective: Solve one-step story problems about parts of a whole.

example.prompt: There are 30 tiles. Exactly 1/5 of them are green. How many tiles are green? Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Write equations for story problems about parts of a whole.
tasks.objective: Write equations for story problems about parts of a whole.

example.prompt: There are 12 tiles. Exactly 1/3 of them are green. How many tiles are green? Write an equation using n for the unknown, then solve it. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: (1/3) × 12 = n; n = 4. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted.
example.solution: (1/3) × 12 = n; n = 4. Equivalent correctly interpreted equations are accepted. Review: Equation models the quantities and unknown in the story. The solution includes the correct quantity.

tasks.title: Write story problems about parts of a whole.
tasks.objective: Write story problems about parts of a whole.

example.prompt: Write your own one-step story problem modeled by (1/4) × 8 = n. Define what n represents and solve your problem. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: One valid example: There are 8 tiles. Exactly 1/4 of them are green. How many tiles are green? Answer: 2.
example.solution: One valid example: There are 8 tiles. Exactly 1/4 of them are green. How many tiles are green? Answer: 2. Review: Story quantities match the equation and requested relationship. Unknown is meaningful and explicitly stated. Solution is 2 with an appropriate unit.

tasks.title: Solve multi-step word problems involving base ten blocks.
tasks.objective: Solve multi-step word problems involving base ten blocks.

example.prompt: A model has 5 hundreds flats, 5 tens rods and 2 ones cubes. Remove 3 tens rods, then add 2 ones cubes. What number is represented? Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Start with 552; subtract 30 and add 2: 524.

tasks.title: Form equivalent fractions by multiplying a fraction by fractions equal to 1.
tasks.objective: Form equivalent fractions by multiplying a fraction by fractions equal to 1.

example.prompt: Create an equivalent fraction to 2/3 by multiplying by 4/4. Show the numerator and denominator before any reduction. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 2/3 × 4/4 = 8/12; 4/4=1. Review: Multiplies numerator and denominator by the same stated factor. Explains that the value is unchanged because the multiplier equals 1.

tasks.title: Reduce a fraction to its lowest terms by dividing the fraction by a fraction equal to 1.
tasks.objective: Reduce a fraction to its lowest terms by dividing the fraction by a fraction equal to 1.

example.prompt: Reduce 45/50 by dividing its numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. Explain why the fraction keeps the same value. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: Divide both by 5: 9/10. Dividing by 5/5=1 keeps its value.
example.solution: Divide both by 5: 9/10. Dividing by 5/5=1 keeps its value. Review: Correct common factor and both divisions shown. Final numerator and denominator are relatively prime.

tasks.title: Given a fraction identify which fractions from a set are not equivalent.
tasks.objective: Given a fraction identify which fractions from a set are not equivalent.

example.prompt: Which fraction is NOT equivalent to 1/3? A: 2/3; B: 1/3; C: 1/3. Enter A, B or C.
example.solution: The nonequivalent value is 2/3; the others reduce to 1/3.

tasks.title: Use the common equivalences in the U.S. Customary System to convert units of weight, length, and liquid measure.
tasks.objective: Use the common equivalences in the U.S. Customary System to convert units of weight, length, and liquid measure.

example.prompt: Convert 9 yards to feet. Use 1 yard = 3 feet. Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Make reasonable estimates of units of weight, length, liquid measure, and temperature in the U.S. Customary System.
tasks.objective: Make reasonable estimates of units of weight, length, liquid measure, and temperature in the U.S. Customary System.

example.prompt: Choose a reasonable estimate for a pencil length. A: 7 inches; B: 7 miles; C: 7 gallons. Enter A, B or C.
example.solution: 7 inches is a plausible everyday estimate for a pencil length.

tasks.title: Identify what percent of a given US customary unit another customary unit represents.
tasks.objective: Identify what percent of a given US customary unit another customary unit represents.

example.prompt: One feet is what percent of one yards? Use 1 yards = 3 feet. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: The fraction is 1/3; multiply by 100 to get 100/3%.

tasks.title: Measure an angle in degrees.
tasks.objective: Measure an angle in degrees.

example.prompt: Read the smaller angle AOB on the protractor, starting from zero on OA. Give degrees. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Use the scale whose zero lies on OA: 70°.

tasks.title: Identify acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles by their measure.
tasks.objective: Identify acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles by their measure.

example.prompt: Classify an angle of 30°: acute, right, obtuse or straight.
example.solution: Compare 30° with 90° and 180°: it is acute.

tasks.title: Use a protractor to measure degrees and draw angles of specified degrees.
tasks.objective: Use a protractor to measure degrees and draw angles of specified degrees.

example.prompt: Read angle AOB, then use a physical protractor to draw a separate angle of 130° on paper. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: 130°; choose the scale beginning at the baseline ray.
example.solution: 130°; choose the scale beginning at the baseline ray. Review: Correct measured angle. New angle has a clearly marked vertex and two rays. Protractor drawing agrees within 2°; use a physical instrument.

tasks.title: Given a fraction of a circle, identify the equivalent corresponding percentage or degree measure.
tasks.objective: Given a fraction of a circle, identify the equivalent corresponding percentage or degree measure.

example.prompt: A sector covers 2/4 of a circle. Give its numerical percent and angle in degrees. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: Multiply 2/4 by 100 and by 360: 50% and 180°.

tasks.title: Name a polygon by the number of its sides.
tasks.objective: Name a polygon by the number of its sides.

example.prompt: Name the polygon by its number of sides.
example.solution: It has 4 sides, so it is a quadrilateral.

tasks.title: Identify a polygon by naming the letters of its vertices.
tasks.objective: Identify a polygon by naming the letters of its vertices.

example.prompt: Name the polygon by listing its vertices in consecutive order. Start at any vertex and go in either direction. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: One correct name is ABC. Cyclic shifts and reverse order are also correct.
example.solution: One correct name is ABC. Cyclic shifts and reverse order are also correct. Review: Visits each vertex once in perimeter order. Does not jump across diagonals.

tasks.title: Identify regular and irregular polygons.
tasks.objective: Identify regular and irregular polygons.

example.prompt: The diagram is drawn to scale. Is this polygon regular or irregular?
example.solution: All sides and all interior angles are equal.

tasks.title: Identify similar figures by comparing their corresponding parts.
tasks.objective: Identify similar figures by comparing their corresponding parts.

example.prompt: Write 10^(7) × 10^(4) as one power of ten. Enter its exponent. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Add exponents: 7+(4)=11.

tasks.title: Multiply numbers written in scientific notation.
tasks.objective: Multiply numbers written in scientific notation.

example.prompt: Multiply (3×10^-4)(9×10^-1) in normalized scientific notation. Enter decimal coefficient; integer exponent. Enter exact decimal or whole-number answers. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: Multiply coefficients 3×9=27; combine powers, then normalize: 2.7×10^-4.

tasks.title: Collect like terms in an algebraic expression.
tasks.objective: Collect like terms in an algebraic expression.

example.prompt: Collect like terms in (7)x + (9) + (-9)x + (8). Write Ax+B by entering A; B. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: x-coefficients: 7+-9=-2; constants: 9+8=17.

tasks.title: Simplify expressions that contain both whole numbers and negative numbers.
tasks.objective: Simplify expressions that contain both whole numbers and negative numbers.

example.prompt: Simplify 2 + (−12) × 2. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Multiply first: (−12)×2=-24; add 2: -22.

tasks.title: Find missing numbers in function tables when a rule of the function is given as an equation.
tasks.objective: Find missing numbers in function tables when a rule of the function is given as an equation.

example.prompt: For y=2x-5, complete y-values for x=-2, 0, 3 in that order. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.

tasks.title: Identify the counting numbers, whole numbers, integers, and rational numbers.
tasks.objective: Identify the counting numbers, whole numbers, integers, and rational numbers.

example.prompt: Name the smallest set containing 0: counting numbers, whole numbers, integers, or rational numbers. Counting starts at 1.
example.solution: Zero is whole but not counting.

tasks.title: Tell how the counting numbers, whole numbers, integers, and rational numbers are related.
tasks.objective: Tell how the counting numbers, whole numbers, integers, and rational numbers are related.

example.prompt: Draw a nesting diagram for counting numbers, whole numbers, integers and rational numbers. Put one example in each newly added region. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: Counting ⊂ whole ⊂ integers ⊂ rational. Examples: 1 in counting; 0 in whole but not counting; −1 in integers but not whole; 1/2 in rational but not integer.
example.solution: Counting ⊂ whole ⊂ integers ⊂ rational. Examples: 1 in counting; 0 in whole but not counting; −1 in integers but not whole; 1/2 in rational but not integer. Review: All inclusions in correct order. Examples belong to the indicated distinct regions.

tasks.objective: Multiply algebraic terms.

example.prompt: Multiply (2x^2y^4)(7x^1y^1). Enter coefficient; exponent of x; exponent of y. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: Multiply coefficients and add exponents of each variable: 14x^3y^5.

tasks.title: Use more than one unit multiplier to convert from one unit to another.
tasks.objective: Use more than one unit multiplier to convert from one unit to another.

example.prompt: Convert 7 yards to inches using two unit multipliers, showing cancellation. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 7 yd × (3 ft/yd) × (12 in/ft) = 252 in. Review: Both multiplier ratios equal 1 as measures. Yards and feet cancel, leaving inches. Correct result 252.

tasks.title: Convert from one unit of area to another.
tasks.objective: Convert from one unit of area to another.

example.prompt: Convert 7 m² to cm². Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Square the linear conversion factor: 1 m²=10000 cm²; multiply by 7.

tasks.title: Draw the diagonals of a polygon.
tasks.objective: Draw the diagonals of a polygon.

example.prompt: Draw every diagonal of this convex polygon, using its labelled vertices. State the number of diagonals. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: 9 diagonals; join all nonadjacent vertex pairs exactly once.
example.solution: 9 diagonals; join all nonadjacent vertex pairs exactly once. Review: No polygon edge counted as a diagonal. No missing or duplicate vertex pair. Correct total.

tasks.title: Find the sum of the measures of the interior angles of a polygon.
tasks.objective: Find the sum of the measures of the interior angles of a polygon.

example.prompt: Find the sum of interior angles of a regular 5-sided polygon, in degrees. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Interior sum = (n−2)×180°: 540°.

tasks.title: Find the measure of each interior angle of a regular polygon.
tasks.objective: Find the measure of each interior angle of a regular polygon.

example.prompt: Find the each interior angle of a regular 10-sided polygon, in degrees. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Interior sum = (n−2)×180°; divide by 10 for one angle: 144°.

tasks.title: Find the sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a polygon.
tasks.objective: Find the sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a polygon.

example.prompt: Find the sum of one consistently directed exterior angle at each vertex of a regular 4-sided polygon, in degrees. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Exterior sum = 360°: 360°.

tasks.title: Find the measure of each exterior angle of a regular polygon.
tasks.objective: Find the measure of each exterior angle of a regular polygon.

example.prompt: Find the each exterior angle supplementary to an interior angle of a regular 4-sided polygon, in degrees. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Exterior sum = 360°; divide by 4 for one angle: 90°.

tasks.title: Solve an equation that has a mixed-number coefficient.
tasks.objective: Solve an equation that has a mixed-number coefficient.

example.prompt: Solve (1 2/3)n = 25/3. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Divide both sides by 5/3: n=5.

tasks.title: Solve an equation that has a negative coefficient.
tasks.objective: Solve an equation that has a negative coefficient.

example.prompt: Solve -9n = 27. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Divide both sides by -9: n=-3.

tasks.objective: Evaluate expressions with negative numbers in place of variables.

example.prompt: Simplify 10 − 15 − 8. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Compute left to right, or add opposites: 10+(-15)+(-8)=-13.

tasks.title: Identify problems that use a percent to describe an amount of change.
tasks.objective: Identify problems that use a percent to describe an amount of change.

example.solution: The percentage compares a difference with an original amount.

tasks.title: Use a ratio box to solve percent of change problems.
tasks.objective: Use a ratio box to solve percent of change problems.

example.prompt: An item originally costs $200. Its price increases by 20%. Use a ratio box to find the new price. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: Original 100% → $200; change 20% → $40; new 120% → $240. Review: Uses the original amount as 100%. Ratio box keeps percentages aligned with amounts. Correct direction and final price.

tasks.title: Solve two-step equations.
tasks.objective: Solve two-step equations.

example.prompt: Solve 6x + (4) = -8. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Subtract 4, then divide by 6: x=-2.

tasks.title: Solve two-step inequalities.
tasks.objective: Solve two-step inequalities.

example.prompt: Solve and graph 8x + (7) < 7. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: x < 0. Open endpoint; shade left. Review: Isolates x and reverses the sign when dividing by a negative coefficient. Graph endpoint and direction match the inequality.

tasks.title: Draw a tree diagram to make a list of outcomes.
tasks.objective: Draw a tree diagram to make a list of outcomes.

example.solution: HH, HT, TH, TT; 4 outcomes. Review: Each stage branches into H and T. Every ordered sequence appears once. Correct total 4.

tasks.title: Find the probability of independent events occurring in a specified order.
tasks.objective: Find the probability of independent events occurring in a specified order.

example.prompt: A fair coin is tossed 5 times independently. What is the probability of heads on every toss? Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).
example.solution: Multiply 1/2 once per toss: 1/32.

tasks.title: Find the probability of dependent events occurring in a specified order.
tasks.objective: Find the probability of dependent events occurring in a specified order.

example.prompt: A bag has 8 red and 2 blue counters. Draw two randomly without replacement. What is the probability both are red, in order? Enter a fraction in lowest terms (or an integer).

tasks.title: Find the volume of a right solid.
tasks.objective: Find the volume of a right solid.

example.prompt: Find the volume of this right circular cylinder in cm³. Use π=3.14. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Base area × height = 3.14×10²×12 = 3768.

tasks.title: Estimate angle measures.
tasks.objective: Estimate angle measures.

example.prompt: Estimate the angle measure without a protractor. Explain the familiar benchmark angles you used. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: The model angle is 105°. Accept a justified estimate within 10°.
example.solution: The model angle is 105°. Accept a justified estimate within 10°. Review: Uses benchmarks such as 45°, 90° or 180°. Estimate is within the stated teacher tolerance; do not require exact measurement.

tasks.title: Use the distributive property to simplify expressions with algebraic terms.
tasks.objective: Use the distributive property to simplify expressions with algebraic terms.

example.prompt: Expand and simplify 6(x + (-4)) + (1)x as Ax+B. Enter A; B. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.

tasks.title: Identify the corresponding angles and corresponding sides of similar triangles.
tasks.objective: Identify the corresponding angles and corresponding sides of similar triangles.

example.prompt: Triangles ABC and DEF are similar in that order. List all corresponding angles and all corresponding sides. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: A↔D, B↔E, C↔F; AB↔DE, BC↔EF, AC↔DF.
example.solution: A↔D, B↔E, C↔F; AB↔DE, BC↔EF, AC↔DF. Review: All three angle pairs and all three side pairs correct. Vertex order preserved.

tasks.title: Use proportions to find the lengths of unknown sides of similar triangles.
tasks.objective: Use proportions to find the lengths of unknown sides of similar triangles.

example.prompt: Similar triangles have AB=4, BC=8, DE=20, and AB corresponds to DE while BC corresponds to EF. Find EF. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Scale factor DE/AB=5; EF=8×5=40.

tasks.title: Use proportions to measure the height of an object indirectly.
tasks.objective: Use proportions to measure the height of an object indirectly.

example.prompt: A vertical pole 2 m tall casts a 4 m shadow. At the same time, a tree casts a 28 m shadow on level ground. Use similar triangles to find the tree height. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: h/28 = 2/4; h=14 m. Review: Corresponding height/shadow ratios consistent. Notes same sunlight angle and vertical objects/level ground. Correct height.

tasks.title: Use a scale to write a proportion to find a measurement on either a model of an object or the actual object.
tasks.objective: Use a scale to write a proportion to find a measurement on either a model of an object or the actual object.

example.prompt: A map scale is 1 cm : 6 km. A route measures 12 cm on the map. Write a proportion and find the actual distance. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 1/6 = 12/d; d=72 km. Review: Consistent map-to-actual units/order. Correct proportion and distance.

tasks.title: Determine the scale factor in a proportion.
tasks.objective: Determine the scale factor in a proportion.

example.prompt: A drawing has a side 3 cm long; its enlarged copy has corresponding side 15 cm. Find the scale factor from drawing to copy. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: New length ÷ original length = 15/3=5.

tasks.title: Use the scale factor to solve a proportion.
tasks.objective: Use the scale factor to solve a proportion.

example.prompt: An enlargement uses scale factor 5. An original side is 5 cm. Find the enlarged side length. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Multiply by the scale factor: 5×5=25.

tasks.title: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the unknown length of a side of a right triangle.
tasks.objective: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the unknown length of a side of a right triangle.

example.prompt: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8 cm. Find its hypotenuse. Enter exact numerical answers without units.

tasks.title: Determine which two consecutive integers the square root of a nonperfect square falls between.
tasks.objective: Determine which two consecutive integers the square root of a nonperfect square falls between.

example.prompt: Between which consecutive integers does √111 lie? Enter lower; upper. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.

tasks.title: Estimate a decimal (or fraction) value for the square root of a nonperfect square.
tasks.objective: Estimate a decimal (or fraction) value for the square root of a nonperfect square.

example.prompt: Estimate √111 to the nearest tenth. Halfway values round up. Enter exact decimal or whole-number answers.
example.solution: Compare squares near 10.5; √111≈10.5.

tasks.title: Show the approximate locations of points representing rational and irrational numbers on a number line.
tasks.objective: Show the approximate locations of points representing rational and irrational numbers on a number line.

example.prompt: Draw a number line from 0 to 5. Mark 1/2 and √6 in their approximate positions; use tenths. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 1/2=0.5; √6≈2.4. Review: Rational point located exactly when possible. Irrational point placed within 0.1 unit of its value. Correct order and equal scale intervals.

tasks.title: Translate mathematical phrases into algebraic form.
tasks.objective: Translate mathematical phrases into algebraic form.

example.prompt: Translate into an algebraic expression: “2 more than 2 times n”. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 2n+2 Review: Operations and grouping preserve the phrase meaning. Equivalent simplified expressions accepted.

tasks.title: Translate geometric relationships into algebraic equations and solve.
tasks.objective: Translate geometric relationships into algebraic equations and solve.

example.prompt: A rectangle is 8 cm longer than it is wide and has perimeter 48 cm. Define a variable, write an equation, and find both dimensions. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: Let w be width. 2w+2(w+8)=48; w=8, length=16.
example.solution: Let w be width. 2w+2(w+8)=48; w=8, length=16. Review: Equation models all four sides. Correct dimensions and perimeter check.

tasks.title: Find the measures of the eight angles formed when a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines.
tasks.objective: Find the measures of the eight angles formed when a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines.

example.prompt: The two horizontal lines are parallel. Angle 1 is 60°. Give angles 2 through 8, in order. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: Vertical/corresponding angles equal 60°; adjacent angles are supplementary, 120°.

tasks.title: Identify the special pairs of angles formed when a transversal intersects a pair of lines.
tasks.objective: Identify the special pairs of angles formed when a transversal intersects a pair of lines.

example.prompt: Name the relationship of angles 1 and 5. Use corresponding, alternate interior, same-side interior or vertical.
example.solution: Angles 1 and 5 are corresponding by their positions.

tasks.objective: Simplify an equation as the first step of the solution.

example.prompt: Solve 2(x+6) + x = 3. Simplify the left side first. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.solution: 2x+12+x = 3; (3)x+12=3; x=-3. Review: Distributes correctly, then combines like terms. Isolates x and checks by substitution.

tasks.objective: Determine if the sign of the product of three or more factors is positive or negative.

example.solution: Cancel factor 2 and 3 factors of x: 4x^3. Review: Cancels matching factors, not terms across addition. Correct remaining coefficient/exponent and nonzero-domain condition.

tasks.title: Find the lengths of semicircles and the areas they enclose.
tasks.objective: Find the lengths of semicircles and the areas they enclose.

example.prompt: A semicircle has radius 11 cm. Find its curved arc length (exclude the diameter); its area. Use π=3.14. Enter exact numerical answers without units. Separate answers with semicolons.
example.solution: Half the circle circumference is πr=34.54; half its area is πr²/2=189.97.

tasks.title: Find the lengths of arcs that are not semicircles.
tasks.objective: Find the lengths of arcs that are not semicircles.

tasks.objective: Find the areas of sectors that are not semicircles.

example.prompt: A circle has radius 5 cm. Find the sector area for a 90° central angle. Use π=3.14. Enter exact numerical answers without units.
example.solution: Take 90/360 of πr²: 157/8 cm².

tasks.objective: Find the two square roots of a positive number.

example.solution: Both (−3)² and 3² equal 9.

tasks.objective: Create and use fraction circles to model and solve problems with fractions and percents.

example.solution: 1; 100%. Review: Equal-size wholes and equal sectors. Shading or annotations distinguish both addends. Sum fraction and percent agree with the shaded amount.

tasks.title: Use fraction circles to model equivalent fractions and percents.

example.solution: 4/5 = 8/10 = 80%. Subdividing each sector into two preserves the shaded area. Review: Both circles use equal sectors. Equal areas shaded. Percent and subdivision explanation correct.

tasks.objective: Use a compass to draw concentric circles.

example.referenceAnswer: Both compass circles share one center; radii 2 cm and 3 cm.
example.solution: Both compass circles share one center; radii 2 cm and 3 cm. Review: Compass center does not move. Radii checked with ruler. Common center labelled.

tasks.title: Use a compass to inscribe regular hexagons and regular triangles in circles.
tasks.objective: Use a compass to inscribe regular hexagons and regular triangles in circles.

example.referenceAnswer: Step the circle radius around its circumference six times. Consecutive points form a regular hexagon; alternate points form an equilateral triangle.
example.solution: Step the circle radius around its circumference six times. Consecutive points form a regular hexagon; alternate points form an equilateral triangle. tasks.title: Use a compass to divide a circle into equal sectors.
tasks.objective: Use a compass to divide a circle into equal sectors.

example.solution: Step the radius around the circumference to mark six points; join each to the center. Six congruent equilateral triangles give central angles 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. Review: Six compass-spaced circumference points. Six radii drawn. Equal-angle explanation with 60° measure.

tasks.objective: Find the measure of inscribed and central angles with a protractor.

example.solution: AOB ≈ 120°; ACB ≈ 60°. The central angle is twice the inscribed angle intercepting the same arc. Review: Uses vertex O for the central angle and C for the inscribed angle. Measurements within 3° when printed without distortion. States the 2:1 relationship.

tasks.title: Pythagorean area proof

example.prompt: Four congruent right triangles with legs a and b and hypotenuse c fit inside a square of side a + b, leaving a central square of side c. Use areas to prove a² + b² = c². Include a labelled sketch. Complete the requested work on paper; this task requires teacher review.
example.referenceAnswer: (a + b)² = 4(ab/2) + c². Expand: a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c². Subtract 2ab to obtain a² + b² = c². The inner angles are right angles because the two acute triangle angles sum to 90°.
example.solution: (a + b)² = 4(ab/2) + c². Expand: a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c². Subtract 2ab to obtain a² + b² = c². The inner angles are right angles because the two acute triangle angles sum to 90°. Review: Sketch has four congruent right triangles and central square. Justifies that the central region is a square. Outer area equals four triangle areas plus c². Algebra cancels 2ab correctly.
